buildable.title: Find the next limit
buildable.question: How far is xs from the receiver creating the same files by itself, and what is it doing with the difference?
buildable.measure: The best arm so far against local tar extraction on the receiver (P2b's local arms; mars now runs macOS, so measured again there), and a profile of both ends during a small-deep fresh copy: sample on macOS, perf on Linux. A quiet sender first: P2b lost runs to its load.
buildable.evidence: P2b, with mars on Linux: 4 local tar processes took 2.70 s on small-deep (about 37k files/s) against 5.26 s for xs in N3.

buildable.title: Re-measure no-op syncs
buildable.question: Where does a no-op re-sync spend its time once the receiver fixes land?
buildable.measure: real-congress and real-psample no-op, push and pull, against rsync; user and kernel time on each end.
buildable.evidence: H21: congress no-op push ran at 0.74x rsync's speed, with 408.8 s of CPU against 18.8 s. MA7's pull deficit came from destination path walks.

trees.question: What limits xs's small-file fresh copies once the receiver's global lock and serial final pass are gone, and what removes the next limit?

nodes.title: Race the receiver-lock branch
nodes.result: fresh 0.411 (faster) / noop 1.007 (inconclusive). The receiver-lock branch (c5b765eb54fc against b02ae2394a86) is clearly faster on fresh copies: 'fresh 0.411 (faster)' with a 95% interval of 0.406 to 0.415 over 8 blocks. That is the minimum block count, but the interval is narrow and far below 1. No-op re-syncs are unchanged within noise: 'noop 1.007 (inconclusive)', interval 0.962 to 1.055. Keep it and merge. The pooled verdicts do not separate the default, --no-atomic and -j8 configurations, so whether extra receiving workers now help is not answered by these facts; A2 should look at that split.

started: Small-file fresh copies are where xs-cpp trails most. Lab races: small-deep.fresh.mac-mars.sender at 24.037 s against xs-rs 9.84 s (rs_vs_cpp 0.409); small-flat.fresh.mac-mars.sender at 13.302 s against 6.528 s (0.491); real-congress.fresh.mac-mars.sender at 32.594 s against 14.723 s (0.452). The branch is already built, so the cost is only race time. Its result also gates A2-A7 and the start point for B1.

$0.07: No race finished this slot; the lab races still show xs-cpp well behind xs-rs on small-file fresh copies (small-deep push 24.037 s vs 9.84 s, ratio 0.409). Next we race A1 (receiver-lock branch c5b765eb54fc), then re-profile no-op re-syncs (B1) on the result. Negative zstd levels (C5) are a low-priority side change.

started: This is lower expected gain on the lab's current workloads. The races are fresh copies on a 10G link where xs-cpp is CPU-bound and trails xs-rs (e.g. small-deep push 24.037 s vs 9.84 s), and Z1 showed level 3 slowing the 10 GbE copy below no compression. Still, it is small, self-contained, and the only buildable change.

$0.05: Splitting the receiver's lock and parallelising its final pass made small fresh copies clearly faster: time to durable fell to 0.411 of the parent's (95% interval 0.406 to 0.415, 8 blocks), while no-op re-syncs were unchanged (1.007, inconclusive). The change stays in the chain, though these results do not yet show whether -j8 helps on its own. Next we profile no-op re-syncs (B1) on real-congress and real-psample, push and pull, against rsync, to find where xs still burns far more CPU than rsync.
